citation: Oosterhof & Todorov (2008), The functional basis of face evaluation
finding: Behavioral studies and a generative face-shape model relate perceived trustworthiness to approach/avoidance valence and resemblance to happy versus angry expressions; dominance is a distinct dimension.
model_implication: Positive/negative affect, brows, mouth curvature, strength and combined cues. These concern impressions, not actual honesty.

citation: Vernon et al. (2014), Modeling first impressions from highly variable facial images
finding: A model using measured facial attributes predicted a substantial portion of variation in impressions of ambient photographs, including approachability; image properties as well as face structure matter.
model_implication: Mouth, eye, shape, pose and image-condition descriptions; do not treat one expression-independent adjective as sufficient.

citation: Gunnery & Ruben (2016), Perceptions of Duchenne and non-Duchenne smiles: A meta-analysis
finding: Duchenne smiles were evaluated more positively overall, including authenticity and trustworthiness; effects depended on stimulus and methodological differences.
model_implication: Cheek raising, eye wrinkles, genuine versus posed or insincere smiles. A visual marker does not prove actual sincerity.

citation: Korb et al. (2014), The Perception and Mimicry of Facial Movements Predict Judgments of Smile Authenticity
finding: Perceived authenticity depends on multiple facial actions and their dynamics, rather than a single static cue.
model_implication: Conflicting eye/mouth expressions and smile qualifiers; motion-related conclusions cannot be tested directly in static faces.

citation: Helwig et al. (2017), Dynamic properties of successful smiles
finding: Judgments of effective, genuine and pleasant smiles depended on combinations of mouth angle, extent, dental show and timing. This is adjacent evidence, not a direct trustworthiness-rating experiment.
model_implication: Dental show, mouth opening, asymmetry and explicit combinations; nonlinear rather than monotonic smile intensity hypotheses.

citation: Sofer et al. (2015), What is typical is good
finding: Along a controlled typicality-attractiveness continuum, trustworthiness peaked around the typical face while attractiveness increased further.
model_implication: Typical, familiar, distinctive and highly attractive captions; smooth nonlinear models and interaction terms.

citation: The Nonlinear and Gender-Related Relationships of Face Attractiveness and Typicality With Perceived Trustworthiness (2021)
finding: This study modeled nonlinear relationships between typicality, attractiveness and trustworthiness and examined differences by gender.
model_implication: Separate attractiveness, typicality and feminine/masculine appearance cues; allow their effects to interact rather than impose fixed signs.

citation: Graham & Ritchie (2019), Making a Spectacle of Yourself
finding: In their experiment sunglasses reduced perceived trustworthiness. Clear glasses and sunglasses should not be treated as equivalent occlusions.
model_implication: Glasses, sunglasses, transparent or dark lenses, visible versus hidden eyes, smiling with eyewear.

citation: Impact of face masks and sunglasses on attractiveness, trustworthiness, and familiarity, and limited time effect: a Japanese sample (2023)
finding: Occlusion and base attractiveness interacted in evaluations in a Japanese sample; eye and mouth coverage have different informational and cultural implications.
model_implication: Occlusion by hair, eyewear and shadows; these experimental and cultural effects are not universal causal coefficients.

citation: Sutherland et al. (2017), Facial first impressions from another angle
finding: Expression and viewpoint affected impressions, with substantial within-person image variability.
model_implication: Pose and expression conjunctions; random-face validation cannot establish accuracy on same-identity latent neighbors.

finding: Downward head tilt increased perceived dominance in their studies through apparent lowered, V-shaped brows. This is evidence about dominance, not a direct universal effect on trust.
model_implication: Head tilt, lowered brows and dominance interactions as exploratory predictors.

finding: Different photographs of the same person produced substantially different first impressions, and image preferences depended on context.
model_implication: Image quality, lighting, view and expression controls; hidden same-person comparisons remain a distinct validation problem.

citation: Todorov et al. (2025), Face evaluation: Findings, methods, and challenges
finding: This review describes contributions from expression resemblance, feminine and baby-faced appearance, shape and reflectance, and substantial perceiver-specific variance in complex judgments.
model_implication: Age, facial maturity, sex-typical appearance, skin reflectance and geometry; interpret group mean prediction without claiming objective personality.

citation: Sofer et al. (2017), For Your Local Eyes Only
finding: The paper examines culture-specific typicality in perceived trustworthiness.
model_implication: Typicality and familiarity may be observer dependent; the model targets this participant sample rather than universal trust judgments.
